component.name: Tailscode
component.summary: Agentes de programación a través de Tailscale
Des agents de code via Tailscale
Tailscale 経由のコーディングエージェント
通过 Tailscale 使用编程智能体
透過 Tailscale 使用程式設計代理

description.p: Tailscode drives the coding agents running on your other machines. The agent stays where your code is; this is the window onto it, over your own tailnet, with nothing in between.
It speaks to Claude Code (through claude-bridge) and to opencode, and it is a native GTK4 application rather than a web view.
What it does:

ul.li: Watch an answer arrive at reading speed, with tool calls, diffs and images inline
Approve or refuse what the agent wants to run, from the conversation
Split the window into panes — several chats, a terminal, the file tree, a browser
See what a conversation has cost and what the month has cost, priced per turn
Read the repository the agent is working in: branch, diff, and what it has touched
Keep every server up to date from inside the app, and be told honestly when it cannot

screenshot.caption: Two conversations side by side, with the file tree
A grid of panes: chats, a terminal and the git surface

description.p: Mac servers ask for Full Disk Access once, and streaming answers take less work.
Mac servers:

ul.li: A server running on a Mac shows whether its agents have Full Disk Access. Without it, macOS stops a turn at a permission dialog on the Mac's screen, where nobody is looking.

One click opens System Settings at Full Disk Access on that Mac, with claude-bridge shown in Finder beside it, and Tailscode notices the moment the switch is on. The first-run dialog asks once when the server it reaches is a Mac; Not now skips it. Needs claude-bridge 1.12.

description.p: Faster:

ul.li: Streaming answers take less work per word in chats with many workflow runs.

description.p: The quick ask no longer crashes, and the Software Updates window stays open.
Fixes:

ul.li: The quick ask (Ctrl+Alt+A) no longer crashes the app a few seconds after it opens when the machine it is aimed at is set to ultracode.
The Software Updates window no longer crashes when a machine's card moves, for example when a restarting bridge stops answering.
A Restart pressed while a server is already restarting follows it back to the version it loads, and a server that doesn't answer says so instead of printing error codes.
The travelling rainbow on an ultracode model pill stops when the desktop turns animations off, and starts again when they come back.

description.p: Undo from here, and provider waits that explain themselves.
opencode 2 chats:

ul.li: Undo from here: right-click one of your messages to wind the chat back to it. The messages after it are set aside, the files the agent changed since are put back, and your words return to the message box to edit. Restore brings it all back until you send your next message.
When a provider is rate limited or out of capacity, the chat shows its reason, which attempt failed and a countdown to the next one, with a button to the fix it names.
Quiet lines show when the model or agent changed, when the server restarted and picked a turn back up, and when a background command finished.
A turn cut off by a server restart can be picked back up or let go, and cost and tokens show for every chat.
Right-clicking one of your messages also offers Copy.

description.p: No more stutter every ten seconds, and faster chats.
Faster:

ul.li: The window no longer freezes for a moment every ten seconds: settings are written only when something changes, in the background, instead of three times a refresh on the thread that draws the window.
Long answers take less work per word as they are written out.
Opening a chat sends all of its requests to the server at the same time and reuses the open connection.
Reopening an unchanged chat no longer downloads it again (needs claude-bridge 1.11).

description.p: opencode 2 conversations stay whole.
opencode 2 fixes:

ul.li: A message you send to an opencode 2 server appears in the chat right away. Before, it could sit under "Waiting for the machine to start" until you left the chat and came back.
A chat where you attached a file opens again. Before, one attachment stopped the whole chat from loading.
Stopping a turn or declining a permission no longer shows an error.
Shell commands run in the same chat from opencode's own terminal appear as they run, and one that timed out or was killed shows as failed.
Files opened by their full path, and folder suggestions for a new chat typed as a full path, work against an opencode 2 server.
The one-line opencode setup script no longer restarts an opencode 2 server in the middle of an answer.

description.p: Server updates show what's new, and the video studio grows up.
Server updates:

ul.li: When a server has a new version, the foot of the sidebar says so. Click it to see what's new before you update.
Each server shows the version it runs, the new one, and what's new in it, with one Update button.
While it updates you see every step — download, build, wait for running chats to finish, restart, confirm — with a timer.
Afterwards it says which version the server is on, even when the server updated itself overnight.
If an update fails you see which step failed and why, and can try again or read the log.

description.p: Video studio:

ul.li: Laid out like the image studio: the form on the left, the clip in the middle, your kept clips on the right.
The prompt helper writes the clip's caption for you, and you can watch the first frame being sketched while it renders.
A clip can start from a picture or continue where a kept clip ended; the image studio's pictures offer Animate this.
A sound field for what the clip should sound like, and an estimate of how long each render will take.
The Fine model is gone. It produced blurry clips, so the studio renders with the one model built for it.
Long prompts scroll inside their box instead of growing the window.

description.p: The prompt helper is chosen, watched and told what it could not see. The studio's helper picker was never on screen; it is now a line under the word count ("with Qwen 3.8 27B") and a chip beside Enhance in a slot, listing every machine that answered — Ollama, llama-swap, llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM — with each model under the name its server gives it, its id, and whether it is already in memory. The default is the best writer rather than the fastest, a model you pick is kept over anything found later, and switching the helper off keeps it filed. A rewrite streams into a card under the words as it is written — Stop while it writes; Use these words, Write again or Keep mine once it lands — with one line for what to change, which sends the same paragraph back for a revision. The helper is told which engine paints, the shape you chose by hand (kept, and answered back), how many reference pictures the words address and that their image tokens must stay, and the avoid list. Taking the paragraph puts it in the box where it can still be edited, with your own sentence one press away.

The picture is watched as it is painted. ComfyUI's own sketch after every sampler step lands on the stage in place of the pulse, captioned Sketch · step k of n, and the finished picture crossfades in over the last sketch instead of snapping into place — the verbs under it already hold their room while it paints, so the stage never jumps as the picture lands. The studio also paints during a render now: it used to rebuild itself for every socket frame and showed nothing until the picture was done. Your ComfyUI needs --preview-method auto (or taesd) to send sketches.

Where a password is typed, the rule is said: claude-bridge, omp-bridge and opencode 2 always want one — BRIDGE_PASSWORD, OMP_PASSWORD, OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD or the one opencode printed when it started — and opencode 1 only if you set one. The add-server form shows it under the field instead of a tooltip, and a server that answers and refuses says the same in its own card.

opencode 2 works. opencode 2.0 rebuilt its whole API — every route moved, every record changed shape, every event was renamed, and a web page answers on every old address — so a 2.0 server used to read as "not an agent server". Tailscode now asks each opencode server which generation it runs and speaks that one: 1.18 and 2.x both connect, list every project's chats in one request, stream answers, tool calls and thoughts as they happen, answer permissions and the new form-style questions, compact, fork and rename, and pick the model, effort and agent per prompt. A server you upgrade under a running app is followed onto its new API without reconnecting. opencode 2 always wants a password — OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD, or the one it prints when it starts — so the connect diagnosis says so instead of promising it needs none, and the one-line setup script now makes a password up when you gave it none and tells you what it is.

The image studio is laid out for a desk: the brief down the left with room for a paragraph — the two engines as cards that say what each is for, the six shapes drawn as the shapes they are, size and detail as segments, the seed and the cutout as switches — the picture in the middle with the machine's own progress narrated over it and the words and verbs under it, and every picture the machine keeps down the right as rows that carry the thumbnail, the words and the facts. An edit keeps the picture it works from on the stage, dimmed, until the result replaces it. The studio, the forge, a design board, the gallery and the delegate desk open the size of the screen, and on KDE they open centred.

Open in browser opens the browser again: a launch goes through GTK's own launcher with this window's display, so an app restarted from a script with no display of its own no longer starts a browser nobody sees. On the proprietary NVIDIA driver WebKit's web process paints on the CPU, which is what stops it dying under every design mock, and a page whose process dies anyway is reloaded once. A build made without WebKitGTK names the package to install for the machine's own package manager and the script that rebuilds, rather than a missing engine; a build made after the engine was installed actually links it.

The image studio asks the model for everything it can actually do. Shape and size are two decisions now: six frames from square to ultra-wide, three sizes up to Qwen-Image-2.1's native 2K, both standing down during an edit because an edit takes its frame from the picture it starts from. One render can work from several references, addressed in the words as <image1> and <image2>, and each one is let go of by the number the prompt calls it. Cutout paints on transparency, Detail trades minutes for steadiness, Avoid keeps things out and says that it costs time, and the seed rolls or holds with one press.

Because this model paints what it is told and invents the rest, a thin brief is now said to be thin, with a frame to fill in, six rules and four worked briefs beside it. Enhance borrows a small model on the machine that paints — Ollama, llama-swap, llama.cpp, LM Studio, anything OpenAI-shaped, found by itself — to write the brief out in the shape the model was trained behind, and pressing it again gives your own sentence back. The chips, the picture's verbs and the shelf are drawn rather than defaulted.

A chat whose agent left a command running that will never finish no longer sits in LIVE NOW as BACKGROUND for the rest of the day. The bridge now reads every background shell against the machine and ends one that has shown no CPU time and no output for ten minutes past the budget the model gave it, saying so in the chat. A row carrying work says how long the machine has been at it, work the server found stuck reads STALLED, and Stop background work in the row's menu ends the work yourself, with the server's reason when it cannot.

Effort levels are the model's own on Oh My Pi. A chat on an omp server was offered Claude Code's ladder, ultracode included, whenever the app could not find its model in the catalog — and it could not find any model reached through a gateway, because the server named it door first while the catalog keeps the door and the id apart. The app now finds the model either way, a model the catalog has never heard of gets omp's own levels from minimal to max, and a model that takes no level shows none instead of the last model's "low".

The archive files what is over and may not hide what is still going. A chat working in the background could be archived and vanish from the sidebar while the phone still listed it; a running turn, a waiting question or background work now keeps the row in the list whatever the archive says, and filing a chat says so.

The archive has a door you can find: its count is the first row of the ⚙ menu, saying nothing was deleted, instead of a button at the foot of a list nobody scrolls to. Shift+E still opens it, and the footer stays for whoever reaches the bottom.

A chat started in the omp terminal is named after its first prompt and says which model it runs the moment it appears in the list, without anyone opening it first; omp-bridge 0.5.5 fixes that at the source.

Model and effort are one dial. The two menus over the composer — one for the model, one for how hard it thinks — are now a single pill: the model's name, the level's word and five bars that light with the heat, from a hollow ember for a model's lowest level up to a rainbow that travels along the word for ultracode. Rolling the wheel over it or pressing Ctrl+Alt+↑ and Ctrl+Alt+↓ steps the level one notch without opening anything, and the wheel stops at the model's lowest level the way it stops at its highest. Click the pill, or press Ctrl+Alt+M, to open the dial: your shortlist and every other machine's models on the left, the model's own ladder on the right. Arrows walk the models and Enter takes one, ← and → and the digits set the level the moment they land, a typed name searches the whole fleet, and the full catalog is one row further down. The pill keeps its width whatever level it says, so nothing shifts under the pointer as you step.

The quick ask wears the same dial for the machine the question is aimed at: Ctrl+Alt+↑↓ steps the level, Alt+M or Alt+E opens the shortlist, and picking a model on another machine aims the question there.

Tables no longer lose their last row. A table was measured before it was in the window, so its columns came out narrower than the text drawn into them; cells wrapped where no fold was planned and the table ran past the bottom of its own card. It is now measured once it is on screen, and every cell's height is counted at the width it actually gets.

An answer no longer appears twice when it finishes. On the Claude bridge the server could hand a finished reply back under a second name, and the app showed both copies until its next refresh — which was also the flash that sometimes ran through the whole chat at the end of a turn. The app now recognises a reply it already holds and keeps a single copy, and claude-bridge 1.8.1 fixes it at the source.

The image studio has the machine's own shelf. Every picture ComfyUI keeps in its output folder — made from this desk, a phone, or the machine's own browser — is listed newest first under the stage, and its words, seed, steps and model are read out of the file itself, so a picture somebody else made still says what made it. Click a tile to put it on the stage with its caption and facts, roll its words again, or start the next render from it without a byte travelling; a shelf read while the machine is asleep is the last one it gave, marked with when. A render is followed on ComfyUI's own socket — loading the model, reading the reference, painting step 12 of 30, decoding, saving — with a bar drawn from the sampler's real count, and Stop takes the render off the machine's queue rather than only ceasing to watch. Klein now genuinely edits from a reference; the fast engine used to paint from words alone while the button said Edit.

Making a picture opens over the work, the way making a video does, rather than splitting the grid for a surface nobody types into; a picture is asked for where words are typed, as a lane on the composer; the chip labelled Generate no longer opens a file dialog; and opening the full-size viewer no longer takes the pointer away from the whole desktop.

Tables are an object with edges. The header is a band, every other row is washed so a wide row can be followed across, columns are measured in points against the pane they are actually in, and while a table is still being written its own card stands in with the count of rows that have landed — then the finished table is washed in on light. The stutter that came with a table arriving a row at a time is gone on every backend, including the Claude bridge, whose messages never said they were still being written.

A sent prompt reaches the top of the window every time: the pin now holds while the answer is still being revealed a glyph at a time, and the room under the prompt is measured against the content rather than against the padding it had just added, which used to ride the prompt down the page and up it.

The model menu has a refresh button, a call that ended has a face that holds perfectly still, a usage bar is drawn against the width it was actually given so a used-up window reads as used up, and a zero in the money column says which zero it is — Local, Plan, Free tier, or Unpriced only where the server never had a rate.

Your servers survive a settings file a newer version wrote. The stored list is read one entry at a time, so a kind of server this build has no case for costs only itself rather than the whole list, and that entry is kept for the next save instead of erased.

Tables are an object with edges: the header is a band, every other row is washed, and the columns are measured in points against the pane they are actually in. A picture is asked for where words are typed — a lane on the composer — and making one opens over the work rather than splitting the grid; the chip labelled Generate no longer opens a file dialog, and opening the viewer no longer takes the pointer away from the whole desktop. A sent prompt's pin holds while the answer is still being revealed, a call that ended holds perfectly still, a usage bar is drawn against the width it was given, and a zero in the money column says which zero it is.

A pane can paint. A split can now hold a picture the way it holds a chat, a page or a stream: name the ComfyUI server that does the work, type what you want, pick quality or speed and a shape, and the pane queues the render and keeps every picture it finishes — newest first, each captioned with the words and the seconds that made it. Hand it a picture instead of a blank canvas and it edits that. It splits, the dividers resize it, zoom hides its siblings, closing it hands the space back, and the layout you leave behind comes back with the machine it painted on and the words it was last given. What it costs is said rather than discovered: the render runs on the machine ComfyUI runs on, not in this pane's grid.

A message you send is on screen from the keystroke. On a conversation of a few thousand rows the transcript fills a chunk at a time, so the row you had just sent had no height to measure yet — the rise to the top of the window gave up waiting, and because it let go of the bottom first, your words sat below the fold until it did. The transcript now stays pinned to the bottom until the prompt can actually be measured, so a send lands the instant it is drawn and rises from there, and the wait runs while the page is still filling rather than against a clock.

Your servers survive a settings file a newer version wrote. The stored list used to be read all at once, so a single server this copy had no case for — a kind added in a later release, or a file carried over from another install — made every server disappear at once, with nothing said, and adding one back then failed outright with a decoding error. Each entry is now read on its own: the servers this build understands are all there, the one it cannot read is left in place rather than erased the next time you add or remove a server, and a list that genuinely cannot be read says so in the log instead of showing you none.

Sending a message puts it at the top of the window, every time. The prompt you just sent rises and the answer streams onto an empty page under it — a rise that used to miss on exactly the conversations where it matters most: a long transcript, a prompt with a picture clipped to it, a message sent again after it failed, the first message in a brand-new chat. The app now waits for the row to be measurable instead of quietly giving the motion up, checks afterwards that the prompt really landed at the top, and puts it back whenever the page moves under it. A tap on the transcript, the keyboard coming up, or the server's own copy of your message replacing yours no longer undoes it.

Tables are readable while they are being written. A row still being typed is no longer drawn with a cell cut in half and rewritten a moment later, a header no longer appears as a line of raw pipes while it waits for the line under it, and a column can widen as the table grows but never narrows — so the rows you are already reading stay where they are. Columns are also sized the same way everywhere now: each asks for its widest cell, the wide ones give way together when the row will not fit, a column of figures is set on one digit width so the numbers line up, and a table too wide for the screen scrolls sideways instead of being squeezed or clipped.

The model menu is what you actually reach for. It used to fill its empty slots with every local model on every server, so two models you had picked sat under six you had never chosen, and the same model appeared twice because a second machine also offered it. It now ends at this chat's model, your stars and your recents — eight of them, enough to fill the menu — with the full directory one row away.

A conversation that is still working on the machine no longer looks finished. When Claude Code starts a long command or an agent in the background and hands you back the prompt, the chat used to go quiet — no spinner, no badge, nothing to say the test it kicked off was still running and that it would come back with the results. Now the server reports the work as long as it runs, and every surface wears it: the chat sits in LIVE NOW with a BACKGROUND pill and a breathing timer badge, the row's second line quotes the task in the agent's own words, the chat's own status reads the count, the orb at the top of Home breathes with one satellite for it, and a screen reader hears that the agent continues on its own when the work ends. The prompt stays open the whole time, because Claude accepts your next message while it waits. Requires the latest claude-bridge on the server; nothing changes for opencode or Oh My Pi, which have no background tasks to report.

A conversation never goes quiet on you again. A turn that ended while the phone was in your pocket, a socket that dropped for a second, a Claude Code turn whose last frame never arrived — each of these used to leave the chat looking busy until you sent something else. The app now keeps its place through a dropped socket and says Reconnecting while it dials again, re-reads the transcript beside every redial so nothing said in between is lost, reads the server's own word on whether a turn is open every time it looks, and redials the moment you come back to a chat instead of waiting for a watchdog.

opencode: a turn waiting on the provider between retries shows as still running rather than as a failure that ends it, and the server's keepalive no longer counts as the conversation speaking, so a turn run by another process on that machine renders live again.
Oh My Pi: a turn the engine dropped is closed on the server's own clock rather than by your next prompt, and an engine that exits mid-turn ends it at once with its reason.

Delegate got easy: picking a class fills the verifier, one sentence under the ladder says where a run starts and how far it climbs, every rung wears its pass rate for that class, a settled run names its next move, a machine with no dispatcher shows the commands that give it one, a run you follow taps your shoulder when it waits for you or ends, and the daemon trusts the tailnet so there is no password to paste.

The quick ask on the Mac and Linux desktops now shows every server as a strip above the field: each machine is a segment named and wearing its agent's symbol, the aimed one selected, and a click or Tab moves the question to the next machine without a menu in between. A fleet too wide for segments becomes one popup. The line under the field says how to send and how to switch.

Slash commands reach the quick ask on Oh My Pi: a server whose commands only ever appeared inside an open chat now publishes its whole catalog — built-ins, skills, extensions and your own command files — the moment / is typed, on every client.

The context ring follows the model you are about to send to: switching models re-reads the same fill against that model's window. A share that rounding would erase reads under one percent instead of zero, and the legend and card titles keep their numbers whole at every width.

Every chat now shows how full the model's context window is. The band above the prompt box wears a ring filled as far as the window is, with the share first and the token count after it, quiet while there is room, amber as it fills and red when a compaction is close. The number is the footprint of the last request the model was actually sent — what it was handed plus what it wrote — never the turn's whole bill, which for a turn of many tool calls is many times the window; a compaction resets it to what survived. The window itself comes from the server's own catalog, so a local model on your own machine is measured against the limit you gave it, and a Claude model reached through Claude Code against its 200k or million-token window.

Tap or click the ring for the whole picture: a large dial with the share inside it, the window banded by what fills it — cache read, cache written, fresh input and the answer — how much is in use, how much is free, which model, where the number came from, what to do about it when the room is getting tight, and Compact one press away.

Delegate hands a bounded piece of work down a ladder of models and reads the result back to you. Write a packet on any server — the class of work, the goal, the files it may touch and the command that proves it — and the dispatcher on that machine tries it on the cheapest tier first, climbs a rung when the check says no, and stops where the work passes. The board shows every tier and what answers there right now, every run with the rungs it failed on and the one it passed at, and the pass rate each class of work has earned per tier, with a hint when a class has proved it can start lower or should start higher.

A run that reaches a gated tier waits for your approval before spending it, and from the run you can cancel it or replay it at another tier to see what a rung is worth. Delegate is part of Pro on iPhone and Mac, and the demo machines carry a scripted dispatcher so you can work the whole feature — approve the run waiting for you, write a packet and watch it climb — before you own a machine that runs one.
On Linux the delegate window, packet dialog and run view are there too, with no Pro needed.

Compacting works on every server. A compaction asked for while the agent is still writing waits behind that turn as a /compact row instead of cutting the answer off, the seam it leaves is drawn with what it traded (tokens before and after, the time it took, the summary behind it), and an Oh My Pi conversation can no longer get stuck busy after one — a message sent into it used to sit there unanswered.

The page glides after the writing instead of jumping a line at a time, a sent prompt rises to the top whichever way the server echoes it, and a fast model is written at its own speed rather than throttled.

The usage screen counts every model, including ones on your own machine that cost nothing, and lets you pick how much of the month you are reading — week, month, quarter or year — with the chart's grain following. A server says what let this device in — trusted through the tailnet, or by its password — and a tailnet-only refusal is never shown as a password prompt.

Clicking through chats is quick and always lands: the sidebar redraws only the row that changed instead of rebuilding the whole list, and never while the mouse is down. Expanding a tool call while the answer is still being written always registers, and a finished conversation holds still — tool marks and workflow circles stop the moment the turn ends.

Answer statistics split the wait the way it actually splits: time to first token is its own figure and tokens per second is measured over the generation that followed, with the model's average on this device behind it. The model chooser explains itself on a right click, a failed tool call closed by hand stays closed, and a workflow card settles the moment every agent has finished.

The answer pushes the page up as it is written. Sending still lifts the prompt to the top of the window, and the transcript now holds still until the written words actually reach the bottom — it used to start scrolling early, chasing text that was laid out but not yet shown. A picture sent with a message rises with the words instead of hiding a line above the top edge, a message sent is on screen the instant it is sent even while the conversation is still loading, and a short conversation no longer reads as already full when a prompt rises.

The model picker starts with the machine: every server is a tab, and under it the providers are a filter — one chip per subscription or key, so you read what Ollama Cloud, OpenCode Go or OpenRouter will run as one list and a pick goes through that door. A model wears its own name (gpt-oss-120b, never a bare GPT), and a heading's chevron always points the way the list is folded.

A queued message belongs to its conversation: it survives a restart, goes the moment its turn yields whichever chat is on screen, and never lands in another chat — switching chats used to carry it along. Oh My Pi conversations name themselves and every Oh My Pi session has a real per-turn ledger; a sent message is drawn exactly like a sent message from the keystroke, and only a failure changes its ink.

Oh My Pi joins Claude Code and opencode as a first-class agent everywhere, Quick Ask aims with real server and model menus, the model directory has stars, Usage has an Ollama Cloud meter, a turn's clock counts from its own prompt, and the jump-to-bottom button is simply the way back.

Ask for a video and watch it being made: an agent renders it on one of your machines while the app follows the work, and the finished film is kept right there. The renderer has its own studio now — one walk sets it up, the model list is a picker you aim into, settings open as a menu, and the chip wears the machine that answered.

The composer grows a third lane beside chat and ask, and the send wears the lane it is sending down. When a provider refuses a request mid-turn, the card says what happened and offers the same words again without the pictures.

A machine that stops answering stops its clocks. A conversation's age counted on whether or not the server holding it was still reachable, so a turn that ended hours ago kept ageing on a laptop that had been asleep since. The column now freezes at the moment that machine was last heard from, and a live card over a server that has gone quiet says so instead of claiming the turn is still running.

A running turn's clock actually runs. The time beside a live conversation only moved when the list was refetched, so it sat still and then jumped. It now counts second by second, without asking any server anything, and holds still the moment there is nothing to count.

New models turn up on their own. A server that had been running for days was still offering the model list it resolved the day it started, so a model your plan gained this week was out of reach until somebody restarted it by hand. The opencode setup command now leaves a check on that machine which notices and restarts it — never in the middle of a turn — and the picker takes the newer list without waiting for a relaunch.

A server can be started over from here. Where a server is explained there is now one press for it, which is the only way back, from the device in your hand, to anything a long-running process reads once at startup: its models, its config, its plugins. It says what it would stop before it does it.

A turn whose machine went says so. A server that stops mid-answer leaves a conversation that reads as a question nobody answered — the prompt is there, no answer follows, and nothing says one was ever coming. It now says what happened, what the work had got through, and offers to pick it back up. And a machine holding a build it has never started is marked in the list rather than hidden behind the trust that keeps it current, because that is work no update will do for you.

Keeping your machines current is the app's job now. A server that already has a newer build sitting on it is one press away from running it, and a machine you trust can take its updates by itself — always waiting until nothing is running on it, so a restart never pulls the floor out from under a turn.

Clearing what you missed now clears it. Notices you had already dealt with came back on their own moments later, because emptying the list left the notifications themselves standing. And the Home screen redraws only the cards that actually changed, so a busy fleet no longer makes it stutter.

A slash command now runs on the model the chat is wearing. Running /command said nothing about which model should answer it, so the server used its own default — and the chat then took that model's name, which is why a conversation could start as one model and quietly become another. Commands, compactions and goals all carry the model and effort named above the box now.

A chat that is connected says so. A conversation nobody was talking in used to sit under "connecting" indefinitely, even while its own transcript, its cost and its branch were all on screen — the app was only ever guessing at the connection from how recently something had been said. It now reads the socket itself, and a connection that really is taking a while counts up so you can see it.

A slash command now runs on the model the chat is wearing. Running /command said nothing about which model should answer it, so the server used its own default — and the chat then took that model's name, which is why a conversation could start as one model and quietly become another. Commands, compactions and goals all carry the model and effort named above the box now.

A chat that is connected says so. A conversation nobody was talking in used to sit under "connecting" indefinitely, even while its own transcript, its cost and its branch were all on screen — the app was only ever guessing at the connection from how recently something had been said. It now reads the socket itself, and a connection that really is taking a while counts up so you can see it.

A turn the machine was pulled out from under is no longer a question that looks ignored. When a server is updated, killed or loses power mid-answer, the chat now says what happened, how far the work actually got — which files were written, what commands ran, how far the answer had come — and offers to pick it back up or let it go.
Typing a folder for a new chat now completes against the real disk on the machine that will host it, the way a shell does: press tab, get the rest of the name.

Chats on a home-directory workspace stream live again. A message sent from Linux or the phone to an opencode session rooted outside the server's project list used to run on the machine — you could watch the GPU work — while the app sat still. The client now finds that session's workspace and follows the turn as it is written.

A turn that comes back with nothing now says so. A model can finish a turn having produced no answer, no tool call and no error at all — most often when the question carried a picture its provider will not take — and until now the whole turn was invisible: the spinner stopped and the transcript sat exactly as it was, as if the question had been ignored. The chat now states what happened, quotes the server's own word for the ending, and offers to ask again — without the picture, when that is what it choked on.

Quick Ask hands its question over properly. Asked at the wrong moment — while another screen was still animating — it could open the conversation and never send the words. The question now travels with the conversation it was asked in, and the sheet slides away onto a chat that is already holding it, in one movement rather than two.
An answer that stopped mid-sentence now finishes.

A streamed reply is played out at reading speed rather than painted in the lumps the network delivers, and a turn that ended at exactly the wrong moment could leave the last paragraph holding half a sentence — with the rest of it already on the phone. The transcript now measures what actually reached the screen instead of trusting the count, and a paragraph it could not hand over whole is tried again until it lands.

The transcript has stopped moving under you. A row keeps its name while its contents change, so a card no longer blinks out and back when the agent revises its plan or a picture finishes loading, and one row changing no longer rebuilds everything under it. Text that arrives while the app is catching up now lands in the paragraph it was being written into rather than above the tools that interrupted it. A code block types out instead of freezing and dumping, and nothing that has reached the screen ever leaves it again.

Type does more of the talking. Your prompt and the answer are set as a question and the paragraph under it — the prompt the heavier voice, the answer the lighter one with the air — a tool's name outweighs its arguments, and every size in the app comes from one ramp rather than a guess per screen. Anything that changes while you watch it is set in figures of equal width, so a settled number no longer reads as movement.

Quick Ask is no longer a text box. Also: tapping a turn-done notification opens the chat instead of closing the app, and a quota banner no longer mistakes a long reply for a spent limit.

Opening a chat now clears its banner along with its row.

Everything since 1.3, in one update.
TROPHIES. Every turn you have ever run is read into a trophy case — achievements, leaderboards and the marks you are closest to earning, with Game Center behind it and nothing to sign up for.

YOUR MONEY, AND YOUR LIMITS. A chat now carries what the whole conversation has spent, and touching it opens the account: per turn, where the money went, which model spent it. The month has its own surface — every machine's ledger merged into one, with your quotas leading on the window that decides when the next send unlocks. And a used-up limit speaks only where it applies: the model picker shows what is spent and when it comes back.

YOUR SERVERS KEEP THEMSELVES CURRENT. The app watches every machine in the picture and wears one quiet mark when an update is waiting — no alert, nothing to dismiss — and one press installs it and follows the server through its own restart.

READING A CONVERSATION. Code is coloured by what it is, in whatever theme you are wearing, and a diff shows its additions and removals. Tables render as real columns. An address written in prose is one you can tap. A picture the agent hands you opens as a gallery you can zoom, save and share. A compaction reads as a seam with its summary a tap away, and the agent's plan is one live board instead of twenty snapshots.

FINDING YOUR WORK. Pin the chats you keep coming back to; a busy row names the tool it is out on, and reads as three facts at three weights. A project opens as its own board. Where a change is landing — the branch, and what has been touched — rides the chrome and opens read-only. Drafts survive leaving a chat.

GETTING STARTED. The app goes and finds your machines instead of asking you to type an address, a chat that cannot start says why and offers the one thing that fixes it, and the install command on the setup screen is the installer.
Plus ultracode, new themes including Suomi, and long-pressing the Home screen icon takes you straight where you were going.
